name: The WEF AI-First Operating System
blurb:
The World Economic Forum published The AI-First Operating System in June 2026, produced with Kearney under its AI-First Enterprises workstream and drawing on more than 50 enterprises and thinkers.

Its central claim is worth stating precisely, because it differs from most enterprise AI guidance. The paper argues that general purpose technologies, electricity, computers, the internet, had limited effect when incumbents applied them inside existing systems, and that the breakthroughs came when firms rebuilt around the technology. It applies the same reading to AI: adopting AI as a tool is a different activity from designing an operating logic around it, and only the second produces the compounding effects the paper describes.

The five building blocks are the intelligence engine, the adaptive AI technology stack, operations redesign, human-AI teaming, and new value creation. The paper extends the traditional business model canvas with AI-first fundamentals so leaders can work through them against their own organisation.

Two things about its framing are unusual and worth noting. The authors state plainly that these blocks are not a transformation roadmap, they are a description of how the frontier already operates. And they concede openly that it remains unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term implications are for productivity, employment and competition. That is more candid than most frameworks in this category.

points.desc: The paper places AI alongside electricity, computers and the internet as a general purpose technology, and argues each had limited impact while incumbents applied it inside existing systems. The breakthroughs came from firms that rebuilt around the technology. That is the distinction between an AI tool programme and an AI-first operating model.
points.name: The thesis: rebuilding beats adopting

points.desc: Intelligence at the centre of operations and business model, so every interaction compounds. The paper breaks it into three loops: speed, scale and scope.
points.name: Block 1: the intelligence engine

points.desc: Modular architecture integrating data, models and workflows, designed to change as the frontier moves. The paper is specific about owning the control layers and keeping a model-agnostic portfolio rather than committing to one provider.
points.name: Block 2: an adaptive technology stack

points.desc: Connecting all operations to the intelligence engine rather than improving workflows at the margins. The paper treats where to allocate intelligence as a deliberate allocation decision, the same way capital is allocated.
points.name: Block 3: operations redesign, not optimisation

points.desc: Roles, teams and structures designed for continuous collaboration between people and AI systems, and an explicit attempt to define what the human contribution is at the frontier rather than leaving it as a residual.
points.name: Block 4: human-AI teaming

points.desc: Every AI-first organisation has to decide how it positions intelligence in the market, from AI as a visible product feature to AI as invisible infrastructure. The paper argues that choice determines where value accrues and how the business competes, which makes it a strategy decision rather than a marketing one.
points.name: Block 5: positioning determines what customers pay for

points.desc: The paper states that the rise of AI-first enterprises is early, that it is unclear which approaches will prove most effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term implications are for productivity, employment and competition. A framework that names its own uncertainty is rarer than it should be, and worth weighing against ones that do not.
points.name: It says what it does not know

reading.body:
The WEF's June 2026 AI-First Operating System argues that adopting AI as a tool and rebuilding an operating model around it are different activities, and only the second compounds.

The paper's analogy is general purpose technologies: electricity, computers, the internet. Each had limited effect while incumbents applied it inside existing systems, and the breakthroughs came from firms that rebuilt around it. The five building blocks follow from that reading. An intelligence engine at the centre of operations, an adaptive stack that stays model-agnostic and owns its control layers, operations redesigned rather than optimised at the margins, human-AI teaming defined explicitly rather than left as a residual, and a deliberate choice about where intelligence sits in the market.

For AI specifically, the stack block is the one with physical consequences. A model-agnostic portfolio and owned control layers imply compute and infrastructure decisions that outlast any single provider, which is a procurement and architecture question before it is a strategy one. The paper does not quantify any of this. It names no compute volumes, no power figures, no costs, and no timelines, so it cannot tell a reader how much capacity an AI-first operating model actually requires or where that capacity comes from.

The framing is drawn from more than 50 enterprises and thinkers, and the authors state plainly that the blocks describe how the frontier already operates rather than a transformation roadmap. They also concede it is unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term effects on productivity, employment and competition will be. That candour is the most useful thing in the document, and it means the five blocks should be read as a description of a small, early set of firms, not as evidence about what works at scale.

The five blocks are not five independent projects. Read together they describe a single dependency chain: the intelligence engine only compounds if the stack can absorb new models without a rebuild, operations redesign only pays if intelligence is allocated deliberately rather than sprinkled across existing workflows, and human-AI teaming only holds if the human contribution is defined before the roles are staffed. The paper's own ordering implies sequence, but it never states one, and the concession that the blocks describe the frontier rather than a roadmap means the sequence has to be inferred from what each block depends on.

The general purpose technology analogy carries a cost the paper does not draw out. Electricity, computers and the internet each took decades to reorganise firms around, and the incumbents that applied them inside existing systems were not lazy, they were rational given what they could see. The same is true now: an enterprise that treats AI as a tool is making a defensible short-horizon decision. The paper's claim is only that the compounding belongs to the other path, and it offers no evidence about how long the gap takes to show up in results.

The stack block is where the paper's silence is loudest for anyone reading it against compute constraints. Model-agnostic portfolios and owned control layers are architecture commitments, and architecture commitments translate into capacity, power and siting decisions. The paper names none of those. It also names no company, no sector and no geography, so a reader cannot tell whether the more than 50 enterprises skew toward firms that already had the capital to rebuild.

What does the paper actually mean by an intelligence engine at the centre of operations?

It means intelligence sits at the centre of both operations and the business model so that every interaction compounds, and the paper breaks this into three loops it calls speed, scale and scope. The data does not define what each loop contains beyond those three words.

Is the model-agnostic stack a technology decision or a procurement decision?

The paper is specific that firms should own the control layers and keep a model-agnostic portfolio rather than committing to one provider. The data does not say what those control layers are, how they are built, or what they cost.

How is operations redesign different from ordinary process improvement?

The paper frames it as connecting all operations to the intelligence engine rather than improving workflows at the margins. It treats where to allocate intelligence as a deliberate allocation decision, the same way capital is allocated, which makes it a resourcing question rather than an efficiency one.

What does the paper say the human contribution actually is?

It says roles, teams and structures should be designed for continuous collaboration between people and AI systems, and that the human contribution should be defined explicitly rather than left as a residual. The data does not say what that contribution is.

Does the paper say how much compute or power an AI-first operating model requires?

No. The data contains no compute volumes, no power figures, no costs and no timelines. Any capacity number attached to this framework would come from outside the document.

Which industries or companies does the framework draw on?

The data says the paper draws on more than 50 enterprises and thinkers but names none of them, and names no sector or geography. It also states that it is unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries or how broadly they will scale, so the framework cannot be used to predict outcomes for a specific sector.

summary: A June 2026 World Economic Forum white paper, with Kearney, describing how enterprises that redesigned around AI actually operate. Five building blocks, drawn from more than 50 companies, and an explicit statement that it is a description of the frontier rather than a roadmap.
